title: The Drifting Hills

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Twelfth Saying: To measure what moves, measure what moves with it.*

The land did not wait for them to be ready. It simply went on, indifferent and slow, moving with the steady, unbothered momentum of a tide that had no shoreline to respect. By the time they had eaten their sandwiches, the stream that had run past the left of their camp had migrated to the right, and the small cairn Joss had built on the ridge was now three feet closer to the path. Isla watched it with the detached, clinical fascination of a doctor observing a symptom. She had measured it. She had marked it. And yet, here it was, having politely shifted its own address while she was not looking.

Joss stood in the middle of the ridge, scratching the sandy hair at the back of his neck, looking at the cairn with the expression of a man whose house had just migrated. "It’s not a hill," he said, sounding faintly defensive, as if the mountain had personally insulted him. "It’s a suggestion. A very large, very stubborn suggestion that it might like to be somewhere else today."

Mags, who was sitting on a rock that had not moved because she had chosen it for its stability, looked up from her porridge. "I’m calling that one Auntie Bess," she said. "And the one behind it is Auntie Prudence. I suspect Prudence is the one doing the moving, just to be difficult."

Isla opened her field-book. The numbers were there, neat and precise, but they were already outdated. In the fixed kingdom of Vell, a measurement was a fact, a thing that existed and stayed existing. Here, in the Unmade, a measurement was a rumor. It was a snapshot of a moment that was already evaporating. She turned the glass toward the next station, a grey peak that looked solid enough to build a house on, but her gut told her it was as unstable as a deck chair on a rocking barge. If she trusted the numbers she had just read, her map would be a lie. And a map that was a lie was worse than no map at all, because it would make people believe they were safe when they were not.

The sun was high, and the heat was beginning to press down on the salt flat, creating a shimmer that made the distant hills look like they were breathing. Isla closed the book. She could not measure the world if she did not understand how it was moving. She looked at Joss, who was still arguing with the cairn, and then at Mags, who was calmly eating her lunch as if the apocalypse were merely a change in the menu. They had to find a way to pin this down. Not by stopping it, but by understanding its rhythm.
pages.image: On a shimmering salt flat, Isla in a mustard coat and green trousers sits on a rock with a field-book, watching a small stone cairn shift slightly on a grassy ridge; Joss in a rust-red shirt stands nearby looking confused, while Mags in a teal jacket sits calmly eating porridge.

pages.text:
The problem was not that the hills moved; it was that they moved at different speeds, in different directions, and at different times of day. If Isla sighted a peak in the morning, it would be one coordinate. If she sighted it in the afternoon, it would be another. The traditional method of triangulation, which relied on fixed points, was useless here. It was like trying to draw a portrait of a man who was constantly changing his face. She needed a reference point that did not move. But nothing in the Unmade did not move. Or so it seemed.

"Look at the ground," Mags said, pointing her spoon at the grey crust of the salt flat. "The salt is old. It’s heavy. It doesn’t have the energy to wander. It’s just sitting there, being boring."

Isla looked down. The salt crust was thin, but beneath it lay a layer of dense, compacted clay. It was the same ground that had held their baseline in the Marches. It was the foundation of the world, even if the surface was a illusion. If the salt-clay was stable, then the hills above it were moving on top of it, like furniture sliding across a floor. The relative distance between two hills might change, but the distance from each hill to the stable ground beneath it should remain constant, provided they measured it all at once.

"Simultaneous sighting," Isla said, the words coming out before she had fully formed the thought. "We don’t measure them one by one. We measure them all together. In the same second. If we lock the angles at the exact same moment, the movement cancels itself out. We capture the shape of the whole slab, not just the pieces."

Joss blinked. "So we need to be in three places at once. And we need to know exactly when to look."

"We need a signal," Isla said. "A flash. A light that tells us the exact moment to read the glass. If we all flash at the same time, we all read at the same time. The geometry holds."

It was a mad idea. It required perfect timing, perfect coordination, and a degree of trust in their own ability to be in the right place at the right time that made Isla’s stomach tighten. But it was the only way to catch a moving target. She looked at the hills, which were creeping silently toward each other, and felt a spark of something she had not felt in Vell. It was not fear. It was the thrill of a challenge that was fair. The land was not trying to trick her; it was simply being what it was. And she was going to meet it on its own terms.
pages.image: Isla and Joss stand on the grey salt flat, Isla pointing at the ground while Joss looks up at a distant hill; the landscape is flat and bright, with a shimmering heat haze rising from the white crust, highlighting the tension between the moving hills and the static ground.

pages.text:
They set up the ring of pegs first. Six of them, driven deep into the clay, forming a perfect hexagon that enclosed the drifting hills. It was a cage made of wood and determination, a frame of reference that said, "Here is where we are. Here is where we are not." Isla checked the angles of the hexagon with her glass, adjusting each peg until the sum of the interior angles was exactly 720 degrees. It was a small, perfect thing, a seed of order planted in the chaos of the drift.

Then they sent Joss and Mags to the far peaks. They carried with them small mirrors, polished until they could reflect the sun back across miles of salt and air. The plan was simple, in theory. Isla would stand in the center of the hexagon, her glass trained on a central marker. Joss and Mags would stand on the highest points of the two most distant hills. At the stroke of the clock, which Isla had synchronized with her chronometer and the position of the sun, they would flash their mirrors. Isla would read the angle to each flash. The light would travel at a speed too fast to drift, so the moment of the flash was the moment of the measurement.

It was a dance of light and time. Isla stood in the center, her breath held, the glass steady under her eye. She watched the sky. The sun was high, a white coin in a blue field. She counted the seconds in her head, a steady rhythm, a heartbeat. One, two, three. The air shimmered. And then, from the two distant peaks, two bright stars flared into existence, sharp and brilliant, cutting through the haze.

She read the angles. Her hand did not tremble. She wrote the numbers down, her pencil scratching on the paper, a sound that seemed loud in the silence of the plain. She checked them. She checked them again. The numbers matched. The geometry held. For the first time in the Unmade, the land had been caught, pinned down, and recorded. It was not fixed, not yet, but it was known. And to know it was the first step toward making it stay.
pages.image: Isla stands in the center of a hexagon of wooden pegs on a salt flat, looking through a brass telescope; in the distance, two bright flashes of reflected sunlight shine from the tops of two separate hills, creating a visual triangle of light.

pages.text:
The first test of their new method went well. The second went better. The third was a disaster, though a funny one, and Isla would remember it for years as the moment the expedition stopped being a task and started being a team.

It happened because of Ledger. The mule, who had been standing patiently behind the tent, had decided that the salt flat was a very interesting place to explore. He had wandered onto a patch of loose ground that was drifting slightly to the east. For the next forty minutes, Ledger simply sat on the hillock, chewing his cud, while the hillock carried him a quarter mile across the plain. He did not move his legs, nor did he change his posture. He simply rode the earth, a passenger on a vehicle he had not asked for.

Isla saw him first. He was a small brown dot, moving slowly against the white background. "Joss," she said. "Get the rope."

Joss ran to the wagon and grabbed the coil of hemp. They had to retrieve him, because a mule who had been carried a quarter mile was a mule who was very, very far from his dinner. They set up a relay, a line of tension that stretched from the stable ground to the drifting hillock. Joss held the anchor end, his boots digging into the clay. Sera, who had been observing with her arms crossed, was forced to join in. "I can do that," she said, her voice tight with indignation. She grabbed the rope, her polished black boots slipping on the loose salt.

They pulled. The hillock resisted, groaning with the sound of earth shifting. Ledger looked up, his ears swiveling, and blinked at them with profound indifference. With a final, concerted heave, the hillock stopped, and they dragged it, and Ledger, back to the stable ground. Sera’s boots were now caked in grey mud, her pristine black leather ruined. She looked down at her feet, and then, against all odds and expectations, she laughed. It was a short, surprised sound, but it was real. She looked at Isla, and for a moment, the mask of superiority slipped, revealing a girl who had just been part of something messy and wonderful.
pages.image: Joss and Sera pull on a thick rope anchored to a small grassy hillock where a brown mule sits calmly; Sera, in a plum coat and muddy black boots, strains with effort while Joss in a rust-red shirt leans back, the salt flat stretching out behind them.

pages.text:
Dusk settled over the plain, the sky deepening from blue to purple, then into a rich indigo. The heat haze vanished as the air cooled, leaving the stars to emerge, one by one, in the darkening vault. Isla sat at the field desk, her lantern lit, and began to plot the hills.

She drew the hexagon of pegs first, a perfect frame. Then, using the angles she had read from the flashes, she calculated the positions of the hilltops. She worked quickly, her pencil flying, the numbers flowing into lines. It was a complex web of geometry, a lattice of triangles and angles that described the shape of the drifting country. As she drew the last line, she stepped back and looked at the sheet.

It was beautiful, precise, and true.

She checked the closure. The sum of the angles around each station was exactly 360 degrees. The lines that should have met did meet. The distances that should have agreed did agree. For the first time in her life, she had mapped a piece of the world that was moving, and she had caught it. The sheet was not just a list of numbers; it was a record of the land’s nature. She felt a swell of pride, a warmth in her chest that had nothing to do with the lamp and everything to do with the work. She was good at this. She was not just an apprentice, not just a scholarship student, not just Corrin. She was a surveyor.

And then she saw it.

At the far edge of the plot, where the lines of the hills ended and the white of the paper began, there was a mark. A thin, faint line, rising from the base of the most distant peak. That was not a hill, nor was it a tree. It was a line of smoke. Thin, grey, and steady, rising into the darkening sky.
pages.image: Isla sits at a wooden desk with a lit lantern, looking at a map sheet with a grid of lines; her expression is one of pride mixed with sudden shock as she stares at a small, faint wisp of smoke drawn on the far edge of the map.
